claims.claim: Born November 26, 1895, in East Dorset, Vermont, to Gilman and Emily Griffith Wilson; younger sister Dorothy; parents divorced when he was 11
Full name William Griffith Wilson; father Gilman Barrows Wilson; died aged 75 of emphysema and pneumonia
After the divorce his father moved to British Columbia and his mother to Boston to study osteopathic medicine

Attended Burr and Burton School in Manchester, Vermont, and Norwich University in Northfield, Vermont; activated before graduation into the Army Coast Artillery Corps in 1917; commissioned second lieutenant
Married Lois Burnham on January 24, 1918, in Brooklyn Heights
Worked on Wall Street as an analyst for brokerage houses; drinking worsened by the end of the 1920s
The couple had no children (ectopic pregnancies, unsuccessful attempts to adopt)
Admitted to Towns Hospital four times in 1933 and 1934 under Dr. William Duncan Silkworth; white light spiritual experience on the final stay
Ebby Thacher visited in late 1934; Wilson entered Towns Hospital on December 11, 1934
Bill got sober with help from Ebby T. under Oxford Group influence; AA began in 1935 in Akron from the meeting of Bill W. and Dr. Bob S., an Akron surgeon
Met Dr. Robert Smith on May 12, 1935; Dr. Bob's last drink June 10, 1935, regarded as AA's inception

Big Book titled Alcoholics Anonymous came off the press in April 1939; Twelve Traditions first printed in 1946; adopted at Cleveland convention July 1950; Twelve Steps and Twelve Traditions published 1953; July 1955 St. Louis handover to the General Service Conference
Wilson was the primary writer of Alcoholics Anonymous, published 1939

Depression since the mid 1940s; first LSD session August 29, 1956, Los Angeles Veterans Administration hospital, with Gerald Heard and Dr. Sidney Cohen; several sessions through 1959; most AA members opposed
Depression in the 1940s and early 1950s; AA board rejected his proposal to recommend LSD and niacin
Met Abram Hoffer in 1960 and promoted niacin (vitamin B3)
Died January 24, 1971, at the Miami Heart Institute in Miami Beach, Florida

Time 100 in 1999; declined Yale honorary degree; heavy smoker; 2021 AA figures of over 120,000 groups and 1.9 million members; Hartigan's claim about Helen Wynn and the 1963 royalty arrangement of 10 percent
Lois co-founded Al-Anon Family Groups in 1951 at Stepping Stones; home purchased in spring 1941
Stepping Stones in Bedford Hills, New York, became a National Historic Landmark in 2012

uncertain: Death place: Wikipedia says Miami; aa.org and an AA timeline say Miami Beach (Miami Heart Institute). Profile uses Miami Beach.
Length of sobriety: Stepping Stones says 35 years, Wikipedia says 36. The profile gives no number.
Cause of death: aa.org says pneumonia; Wikipedia says emphysema and pneumonia.
Towns Hospital admissions: Wikipedia's wording puts four stays in 1933 to 1934; exact dates of the first three were not confirmed.
The December 1934 experience: Wikipedia notes he was being given belladonna at the time, and some attribute the experience to it. Left out of the prose as interpretation.

Depression dates: sources say 'mid-forties' onward or '1940s and early 1950s'; the often cited 1944 to 1955 range was not confirmed on a fetched page. Wikipedia also describes earlier episodes from age 17.
When LSD sessions ended: 1959 per one source, possibly into the early 1960s per others.
The Helen Wynn affair rests on biographer Francis Hartigan's account as reported by Wikipedia; the book itself was not fetched.
No quote included: no primary text with his exact words was fetched (aa.org timeline page returned no body, Britannica blocked).
Publication year 1984 for Pass It On was not confirmed on a fetched page; the title was cited by a fetched secondary article.
Reported whiskey requests in his final weeks (Wikipedia, citing a nurse's notes) were left out as thinly sourced.
